explanation: First locate the node by its Data value. Its successor is the leftmost node in its right subtree, if that subtree exists; otherwise climb Parent links until leaving a left child. No such ancestor means no successor.
timeComplexity: O(n) time to locate the node, then O(h) to find its successor. Native functions begin at the target, while C#/JavaScript first search the tree to resolve its data identifier.
spaceComplexity: O(h) auxiliary search stack for tree height h. C#/JavaScript use a height-sized DFS stack to locate the target; native code begins with the node and needs only a cursor.
attribution: JavaScript port of the independently authored EPI Practice C# algorithm; no upstream reference code copied.
correctness: The initial search identifies the node by Data, as required by this contract. If it has a right subtree, that subtree’s leftmost node is the first later node in inorder. Otherwise inorder must ascend: ancestors reached from a right child were already visited, while the first ancestor reached from its left child has not been visited and is next. Reaching above the root proves there is no successor.
walkthrough: In tree [14, 6, 22, 3, 9, 18, 27, null, 4], find the node whose Data is 9. It has no right subtree. Climb to 6, which was reached from its right child, then to 14, reached from its left child. The first such ancestor is 14, so return 14. JSON arguments are [tree,nodeData]. Native wrappers resolve the node and call the one-node function; C#/JavaScript receive tree and data.
edgeCases: A node with a right subtree uses that subtree’s leftmost descendant.
The last inorder node has no successor and returns -1.
node_idx is a Data value, not a zero-based traversal position.
